ai-at-work.title: PitchBook: US venture funding hits $412.7B in first half as AI deals dominate
ai-at-work.excerpt: U.S. venture capital deal value hit $412.7 billion in the first half of 2026, nearly 30% more than investors put to work in all of last year — and a small cluster of giant artificial intelligence roun
ai-at-work.dwp_take: US venture capital hit $412.7 billion in the first half of 2026, with AI deals driving nearly all the growth compared to last year's total funding. Digital workplace professionals need to pay attention because this capital flood means AI-powered workplace tools are about to hit the market at scale, and your organization will be expected to adopt them whether you're ready or not. Here's the thing though: just because money is pouring into AI doesn't mean those solutions will actually solve the problems keeping your employees productive and sane at work.

ai-at-work.title: Meta reportedly testing prototype AI specs that record everything the user sees and hears
ai-at-work.excerpt: Meta Platforms Inc. this week sought to reassure consumers about the privacy safeguards of its controversial artificial intelligence-enabled glasses, yet at the same time it’s reportedly pushing even
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Meta is building prototype AI glasses that record everything users see and hear while claiming to have privacy safeguards in place. This matters because these devices could become standard workplace tools, and if they're already causing privacy backlash in consumer markets, imagine the employee relations nightmare when someone walks into a meeting wearing one of these things. Meta's approach of saying "trust us, privacy is important" while simultaneously building creepier prototypes is peak tech company theater, and I've seen this movie before.

ai-at-work.title: Blue Origin seeks to raise $10B from external investors in first VC-led funding round
ai-at-work.excerpt: Jeff Bezos’s rocket company Blue Origin Enterprises LP is reportedly looking to raise money from outside investors for the first time in more than two decades. The company is in talks to secure $10 bi
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Blue Origin is finally opening its wallet to outside investors after twenty years of Bezos footing the bill solo, aiming to raise $10 billion at a $130 billion valuation. For digital workplace folks, this signals how even the most well-funded private companies eventually need external capital and the accountability structures that come with it. Turns out even billionaires realize you can't just bootstrap your way to Mars forever without someone asking uncomfortable questions about your burn rate.

ai-at-work.dwp_take: Prime Intellect pulled in $130 million from heavy hitters like Nvidia and Intel to build AI training platforms, hitting a $1 billion valuation in the process. The funny part is that in six months someone will definitely ask you why your company isn't using Prime Intellect yet, despite nobody actually knowing what it does.

tools-tech.title: The next killer AI feature? No AI at all

tools-tech.dwp_take: Computerworld's piece argues that the most compelling product strategy right now might actually be restraint, building tools that work without AI rather than jamming it into everything. This matters because digital workplace leaders are getting hammered by executives demanding AI integration while their teams are drowning in half-baked chatbots that nobody asked for. After three decades in this space, I can tell you the best feature is still a tool that solves a real problem, and sometimes that tool doesn't need a neural network to do it.

tools-tech.title: OpenAI to release delayed models Thursday amidst a sea of regulatory confusion
tools-tech.excerpt: As enterprises struggle to manage their AI strategies, the US AI regulatory environment is sending a wide range of contradictory signals. OpenAI’s Wednesday announcement that it will now release GPT-5
tools-tech.dwp_take: OpenAI is dropping new AI models Thursday despite the US government reportedly asking them to hold back access to their top models, creating a regulatory mess nobody quite understands. This matters because digital workplace teams are trying to build AI policies and governance frameworks while the rulebook keeps changing mid-game. Honestly, it's like being asked to drive safely while someone keeps moving the speed limit signs around, which explains why most enterprises are just waiting to see what happens before committing to anything.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft hopes to cut its genAI costs by focusing on its own models
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft plans to focus more on in-house AI models in an effort to reduce its costs for generative AI (genAI), Bloomberg reports. The company has begun using its own MAI models to handle some user AI
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft is shifting its Copilot strategy to rely more on its own AI models instead of outsourcing everything to OpenAI and Anthropic, which should cut their genAI costs considerably. This matters because it signals that the real economics of enterprise AI are finally forcing vendors to get serious about efficiency rather than just bolting on the shiniest third-party models. After years of treating genAI like a free lunch, Microsoft's pivot to homegrown solutions tells you everything you need to know: the actual cost of running this stuff at scale is a real problem nobody wants to admit.

tools-tech.title: The $2,000 club: Apple, Samsung, Google bet on foldables
tools-tech.excerpt: Apple, Samsung, and Google are all expected to introduce their takes on folding smartphones in the coming weeks. All three competitors work together on some things; Samsung allegedly makes displays fo
tools-tech.dwp_take: Apple, Samsung, and Google are all launching foldable phones in the coming weeks, with all three devices expected to hit that $2,000 price point. For digital workplace professionals, this matters because foldables are finally becoming mainstream tools rather than novelties, which means IT teams need to start thinking about device management, app compatibility, and security policies for a screen format most organizations haven't dealt with yet. Here's the thing though: we've been hearing about foldables being the future for five years, and they're still expensive toys for early adopters, so don't expect your average office worker to ditch their iPhone 15 anytime soon.

digital-culture.title: These moms ditched corporate life to buy their own businesses
digital-culture.excerpt: For Anica John, the pandemic was a revelation. At the beginning of the lockdown, she had a 5-year-old child and worked in product management at Walmart Labs. John, whose husband is a professor at Stan
digital-culture.dwp_take: A group of women, including a former Amazon product manager, left corporate jobs during and after the pandemic to start their own businesses, citing the incompatibility of demanding office cultures with parenting responsibilities. This matters to digital workplace leaders because it exposes a real talent drain: companies are losing experienced professionals not because they lack ambition, but because rigid return-to-office policies make their lives unsustainable. Here's the thing: if your RTO mandate is so inflexible that it drives away talented people with families, maybe the problem isn't remote work culture, it's your leadership's inability to design work that actually fits how humans live.

digital-culture.title: What Microsoft is offering laid-off employees in severance
digital-culture.excerpt: After announcing layoffs that impact 2.1% of its global workforce, Microsoft is providing most U.S. employees up to 39 weeks of base pay, according to severance offers reviewed by Business Insider. Th
digital-culture.dwp_take: Microsoft is offering laid-off US employees between 60 days and 39 weeks of base pay depending on tenure, affecting 2.1% of their global workforce. This matters because it sets a baseline expectation for how tech companies should handle workforce reductions, and your organization will face questions about whether your severance compares fairly. Honestly, 39 weeks is generous by industry standards, which either means Microsoft feels guilty or they're trying to avoid becoming a cautionary tale on social media.

digital-culture.title: The Imagination Era: Why creativity matters more than ever in the age of AI
digital-culture.excerpt: We are entering what the creativity strategist Natalie Nixon calls the Imagination Era, a moment when ideas, curiosity, and new ways of thinking matter more than ever. As artificial intelligence accel
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company is arguing that as AI handles routine work, human creativity becomes the actual competitive advantage worth fighting for, and leaders need to position AI as a thinking partner rather than a threat. This matters to digital workplace folks because we're the ones building the systems and cultures that either unlock creative collaboration or accidentally turn knowledge workers into prompt typists. The irony is that most organizations are still struggling to get basic collaboration right, so treating AI as a "creative partner" might be putting the cart before a horse they haven't even learned to ride yet.

digital-culture.title: ADHD brains are prone to wandering. That’s a secret weapon in the workplace
digital-culture.excerpt: Some of the symptoms that create challenges for those with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may also contribute to a greater capacity for creativity under the right circumstances. Trait
digital-culture.dwp_take:
Here's my take:

Fast Company argues that ADHD traits like distractibility and daydreaming can actually fuel creativity and innovation when properly supported in work environments. This matters because digital workplace leaders are finally realizing that neurodivergent employees aren't broken versions of neurotypical workers, they're just wired differently and often bring genuine creative advantages. The real trick isn't celebrating ADHD as some magical creativity pill, it's building flexible work systems that let these brains do what they do best instead of forcing everyone into the same rigid productivity theater.

industry-news.title: The AI Security Gap No One’s Watching in Australian Enterprises
industry-news.excerpt: New global security research shows exactly how unmonitored AI agent permissions get exploited inside the enterprise — and Australian identity governance, built around human employees, isn't set up to
industry-news.dwp_take: Australian enterprises are running AI agents with permissions nobody's actually watching or controlling because their identity governance systems were designed for humans, not autonomous software. This matters because unmonitored AI agents represent a whole new attack surface that traditional security frameworks can't see coming, and when something goes wrong, nobody knows what permissions it had or what it accessed. After three decades in this space, I can tell you that "we'll figure out the security later" has never once ended well, and yet here we are again with the same tape playing on repeat.

industry-news.title: Windows 11 Cleanup Guide: 9 Ways to Make Your PC Feel Faster

Here's the thing: most of these tips are just basic hygiene that should have been done in the first place, but I'll take it over another article about AI solving workplace problems that don't exist.
